getting-started.script:
New puppy at home? Cute face, tiny paws... and a surprising number of toilet trips. Take them out when they wake up, after food or play, and before bed. Very young pups may need another trip every forty-five minutes to an hour while they're awake. Had an accident? It happens. Skip the telling-off, clean up, and try again. When they go in the right spot, reward them straight away. You're both learning.

Now, meals. Blue Cross suggests four a day from eight weeks to four months, three until six months, then two. That's a starting point to check with your vet, especially with a very small pup. Measure the whole day's food first, then split it between meals. Keep fresh water available.

And yes, there's a lot of sleeping. Young puppies often clock up around eighteen to twenty hours across the whole day, naps included. Give them a quiet spot to rest, and some company while they settle in. You may still be doing a few overnight toilet trips.

For this first week, book a vet check, sort out vaccination and parasite advice, and get the house puppy-ready. Start little, gentle introductions to everyday life. Before heading to new places or meeting dogs, ask your vet what's safe while vaccinations are still in progress.

The written guide has the sources and more detail. Your vet can help tailor this advice to your puppy.
getting-started.sourceText:
Your first days with a puppy

Start here: potty breaks, meals, naps, and a manageable first week.

Potty: little and often

Offer a toilet trip on waking, after food or play, and before bed. Very young puppies may need another trip every 45–60 minutes while awake. Watch their signals and reward them at the toilet spot.

Meals: small and regular

Blue Cross suggests four meals daily at 8 weeks to 4 months, three at 4–6 months, then two. Divide the daily food allowance between meals; keep fresh water available. Confirm the plan with your vet, especially for very small puppies.

Sleep: make room for naps

Young puppies often sleep around 18–20 hours over a whole day. Provide a quiet resting place and company while they settle into their new home. Expect some overnight toilet trips.

This week

Arrange a vet check, confirm vaccines and parasite care, and puppy-proof your home. Start brief, gentle, rewarding introductions to everyday life. Ask your vet which places and dogs are safe before vaccinations are complete.

This is a Puptime puppy care summary. Ask your vet about health, diet, and vaccination decisions. Sources and further reading are available in the written guide.

bringing-puppy-home.script:
Before the big homecoming, give your puppy a small, safe place to land. Somewhere easy to clean, with a comfy bed, water, and enough room to move around. Gates or a pen can help you keep an eye on things.

Then take a look around for anything a curious mouth could get into. Cables, medicines, cleaning products, and little things they could swallow all need to be out of reach. Have a look at the garden too. Any gaps they could squeeze through?

For the practical bits, have their usual food ready, along with bowls, bedding, suitable toys, a lead, and a collar or harness that fits. Poo bags and cleaning supplies will get plenty of use. Ask the breeder or rescue for feeding details, vaccination and worming records, and, if possible, something that smells familiar.

When they arrive, keep the day fairly quiet. A few people and a few spaces at a time is plenty. Give them chances to go to the toilet and have a rest between introductions.

If you'll be out, arrange someone to help with meals, toilet trips, and company. A pen can make an area safer, but your puppy still needs you to help them settle and learn about being alone gradually.

The written guide has the sources and more detail. Your vet can help tailor this advice to your puppy.
bringing-puppy-home.sourceText:
Before your puppy comes home

A safe space, useful supplies, and a plan for the first day.

Prepare a small, safe area

Choose somewhere easy to clean with a comfortable bed, water, and space to move. Use gates or a pen to limit access to hazards. Put cables, medicines, cleaning products, and small swallowable objects out of reach. Check the garden for escape routes.

Have the basics ready

Bring home the food your puppy already eats, bowls, bedding, suitable toys, a lead and well-fitting collar or harness, poo bags, and cleaning supplies. Ask for vaccination and worming records, feeding details, and something familiar-smelling if available.

Plan for company

Keep the first day calm. Introduce a few spaces and people at a time, with opportunities to toilet and rest. Arrange help with meals and toilet trips if you will be away. A safe enclosure does not replace company or gradual alone-time training.

This is a Puptime puppy care summary. Ask your vet about health, diet, and vaccination decisions. Sources and further reading are available in the written guide.

toilet-training.script:
Let's talk about all those trips outside. For a very young puppy, start with plenty of chances to go. The RSPCA suggests roughly every forty-five minutes to an hour, depending on age. Battersea also describes hourly trips at first. Dogs Trust gives a broader two-hour routine, with extra trips after activities. So you'll see different starting points in the advice. None of them guarantees how long your own puppy can wait.

For a tiny pup, start with the shorter gap and watch what actually happens. Take them out when they wake up, after food or play, and before bed, even if the next trip isn't due yet. Sniffing around, circling, getting restless, or heading for the door? That's your cue to go now.

Pick a safe, consistent spot and stay with them. Give them a moment. As soon as they've finished in the right place, reward them there. If nothing happens, head back in, keep an eye on them, and try again soon.

Accidents happen. Skip the telling-off and clean up properly with a pet-safe enzymatic cleaner. Some pups need overnight trips too. Keep those quiet, then settle back to bed. Keep water available; taking it away to prevent accidents isn't the answer.

Logging pees and poops in Puptime can help you notice a pattern. A reminder just means it's time to check. If your puppy needs to go sooner, go sooner. And if things suddenly change, or they seem uncomfortable or strain to go, speak to your vet.

The written guide has the sources and more detail. Your vet can help tailor this advice to your puppy.
toilet-training.sourceText:
How often does a puppy need to go out?

Frequent trips, signals to watch for, and what to do about accidents.

Start with frequent opportunities

The RSPCA suggests trips every 45 minutes to an hour, depending on age; Battersea notes that puppies often need hourly trips initially. Dogs Trust offers a broader two-hour routine plus trips after activities. These are starting points, not bladder guarantees. Begin with the shorter interval for a very young puppy and adjust to what actually happens.

Go out on waking, after eating or playing, and before bed, even if the next planned trip is not due. Sniffing the floor, circling, restlessness, or heading to the door are reasons to go now.

Help them get it right

Use a consistent, safe toilet spot. Stay with your puppy, give them time, and reward them there immediately after they finish. If nothing happens, return indoors, supervise, and try again soon. Do not punish accidents; clean the area thoroughly with a pet-safe enzymatic cleaner.

Nights and setbacks

Some puppies need overnight trips. Keep them quiet and return to bed afterwards. Keep water available rather than restricting it to prevent accidents. Sudden changes, straining, or discomfort need vet advice.

Log actual pees and poops in Puptime to spot your puppy’s pattern. A reminder is a prompt to check, not proof they can wait; do not wait for a notification when they show a need.

This is a Puptime puppy care summary. Ask your vet about health, diet, and vaccination decisions. Sources and further reading are available in the written guide.

feeding.script:
One of the first surprises with a puppy is how often breakfast seems to come around. For a pup coming home at about eight weeks, Blue Cross suggests four meals a day until four months, three until six months, then two. The Royal Kennel Club's timings differ a little: four meals at two to three months, two or three at four to six months, then two, depending on breed. Have a chat with your vet about the right transition for your puppy.

Space the meals fairly evenly through the day. Very small pups, or pups with health problems, may need a different plan. Start with the food they're already eating, and make any change gradually.

Here's an easy detail to miss on the packet: that allowance is usually for the whole day. Measure it, then divide it between meals. Check whether the guide uses your puppy's current weight or their expected adult weight. Choose a complete puppy food suited to their expected adult size, and review their growth and body condition with your vet. Large-breed puppies need particular care with growth nutrition.

Training treats count towards the day's food too. You can use some of their measured kibble for rewards. Don't add supplements to a complete diet unless your vet recommends them.

Keep fresh water available day and night. Offer food somewhere calm, and avoid strenuous exercise close to meals. Keep a note of meal times and appetite changes. If your puppy seems unwell or stops eating, check with your vet rather than just moving meals around.

The written guide has the sources and more detail. Your vet can help tailor this advice to your puppy.
feeding.sourceText:
How often and how much should a puppy eat?

Meal frequency by age, daily portions, treats, and water.

A starting point for meal frequency

For puppies coming home at about 8 weeks, Blue Cross recommends four meals a day until 4 months, three until 6 months, then two. The Royal Kennel Club gives four meals at 2–3 months, two to three at 4–6 months, then two depending on breed. Ask your vet which transition suits your puppy.

Space meals fairly evenly through the day. Very small puppies and puppies with health problems may need a different plan. Keep their existing food initially and introduce a change gradually.

The daily allowance is not a per-meal allowance

Choose a complete puppy food suitable for their expected adult size. Read whether the packet’s guide uses current weight or expected adult weight. Measure the daily amount, then divide it between meals. The label is a starting point: review growth and body condition with your vet.

Count training treats as part of the day’s food. Using some of the measured kibble allowance for training can help. Do not add supplements to a complete diet unless your vet recommends them. Large-breed puppies need particular attention to growth nutrition.

Water and meal habits

Provide fresh water throughout the day and night. Offer food somewhere calm and avoid strenuous exercise close to meals. Record meal times and appetite changes; if your puppy seems unwell or stops eating, ask your vet rather than simply changing the schedule.

This is a Puptime puppy care summary. Ask your vet about health, diet, and vaccination decisions. Sources and further reading are available in the written guide.

sleep-and-first-nights.script:
Puppies can be wonderfully busy... and then need an awful lot of sleep. The American Kennel Club describes around eighteen to twenty hours across the day for young pups, including naps. Think of that as a broad guide. You don't need to make them hit a sleep target.

Give them plenty of quiet chances to rest between little bursts of playing, eating, learning, and toilet trips. If your puppy gets extra bitey or seems to get busier and busier, they might be overtired. Try a calmer space and a chance to settle before adding more exercise.

Those first nights can feel strange for them. They've just left familiar people or littermates. Blue Cross and Dogs Trust suggest staying nearby at first. You could put their bed near yours, or sleep near their resting area for a while. If it suits your home, gradually increase the distance as they get comfortable.

Offer a toilet trip before bed. If they wake and need to go, keep it quiet, then help them settle again. Check what they need if they're upset, rather than leaving them distressed for a long time.

And a crate is optional. A bed, pen, or puppy-proofed area can work too. If you do use a crate, build up positive experiences with it. A puppy who hasn't met one before needs a gentle introduction before spending a night in it. It should feel like a resting place, never a punishment.

The written guide has the sources and more detail. Your vet can help tailor this advice to your puppy.
sleep-and-first-nights.sourceText:
Naps, bedtime, and the first few nights

Lots of sleep, a calm resting place, and help settling at night.

Expect a lot of sleep

The American Kennel Club describes around 18–20 hours of sleep per day for young puppies, including naps. This is a broad expectation, not a quota to force. Give them frequent chances to rest undisturbed between short periods of play, eating, training, and toileting.

An overtired puppy may get busier or mouthier. More exercise is not always the answer. Try a quieter environment and an opportunity to settle.

Stay nearby while they settle

Your puppy has just left familiar people or littermates. Blue Cross and Dogs Trust advise being nearby at first. Put their bed near yours or temporarily sleep near their resting area, then increase distance gradually if that suits your household.

Offer a toilet trip before bed. If they wake and need to go, make it a calm trip and settle them again. Check distress and practical needs rather than leaving them to cry for long periods.

A crate is optional

A bed, pen, or puppy-proofed area can work. If you choose a crate, introduce it gradually with positive experiences; do not immediately shut an unfamiliar puppy inside overnight. It should be a resting place, never a punishment.

This is a Puptime puppy care summary. Ask your vet about health, diet, and vaccination decisions. Sources and further reading are available in the written guide.

exercise-and-play.script:
A puppy walk can involve quite a lot of stopping to sniff the same patch of grass. That's part of the experience. PDSA recommends a mix of gentle play, short walks, and training while puppies grow. Let them go at their own pace, with time to sniff and rest.

Keep things low-impact. Avoid forced runs, repeated jumping, and skidding around, especially while their joints are developing.

You might have heard the rule about five minutes of exercise for every month of age. It's easy to remember, but it isn't a proven scientific limit. PDSA says it isn't appropriate for most puppies. Breed, size, health, age, and what they're actually doing all matter. Your vet can help you work out what suits your pup.

While vaccinations are still in progress, ask which outdoor places are safe locally. You can still do home play and safe, controlled introductions to everyday sights and sounds while waiting for clearance for public walks. Avoid dog parks and places used by dogs whose vaccination status you don't know.

There are plenty of little ways to keep their brain busy too. Try short reward-based training, sniffing games, or a suitable food puzzle. Use food from their daily allowance, supervise toys and chews, and leave room for naps. If moving seems painful, or your puppy gets unusually tired, stop and ask your vet.

The written guide has the sources and more detail. Your vet can help tailor this advice to your puppy.
exercise-and-play.sourceText:
Exercise, walks, and play without overdoing it

Gentle exploration and rest, with advice tailored to your puppy.

Quality matters more than a stopwatch

PDSA recommends a balance of play, short walks, and training while puppies develop. Choose low-impact activity at their pace, with time to sniff and rest. Avoid forced runs, repeated jumping, and skidding, especially while joints are growing.

The familiar “five minutes per month of age” rule is not a proven scientific limit. PDSA explicitly notes that it is not appropriate for most puppies. Age, breed, size, health, and the activity itself matter; ask your vet for individual guidance.

Exercise before vaccinations are complete

Ask your vet which outdoor areas are safe locally. Home play and safe, controlled exposure to everyday sights and sounds can begin while you wait for clearance for public walks. Avoid dog parks and places used by dogs with unknown vaccination status.

Give the brain something to do

Short reward-based training, sniffing games, and suitable food puzzles offer variety. Use food from the day’s allowance, supervise toys and chews, and leave room for naps. Stop and seek advice if movement seems painful or your puppy becomes unusually tired.

This is a Puptime puppy care summary. Ask your vet about health, diet, and vaccination decisions. Sources and further reading are available in the written guide.

socialisation.script:
Socialisation can sound like a very big to-do list. People, dogs, traffic, the hoover... where do you start? With little experiences your puppy can feel comfortable with. AVSAB, the veterinary behaviour society, highlights the first three months as an especially important learning period.

Let your puppy watch things from a comfortable distance. Pair new experiences with something they enjoy, and keep it short. They don't need to greet every dog or meet everyone at once. If they freeze, hide, try to get away, or look overwhelmed, give them more space and make it easier. Don't force the introduction.

There's a balance to find while vaccinations are still in progress. AVSAB supports safe early socialisation, while avoiding higher-risk places such as dog parks. Ask your vet about local disease risks, safe outings where you carry your puppy, and meeting known healthy, vaccinated dogs.

Thinking about a puppy class? AVSAB says a well-run class may start at seven to eight weeks, with at least one vaccine set given at least seven days beforehand, and an initial deworming. That isn't automatic permission to attend. Your vet and the class provider need to agree that your puppy's health and their requirements make it appropriate.

At home, introduce sounds, gentle visitors, handling, and car travel a little at a time. Look for classes that use rewards and let puppies take a break. You can keep building confidence as they grow. There's no need to rush through a whole checklist in a week.

The written guide has the sources and more detail. Your vet can help tailor this advice to your puppy.
socialisation.sourceText:
Socialisation: safe, positive introductions

Introduce the world gently, including before all vaccinations are finished.

Start early, keep it comfortable

AVSAB identifies the first three months as an especially important socialisation period. Socialisation means building comfortable responses to people, animals, handling, sounds, surfaces, and environments. It does not mean greeting every dog or tolerating overwhelming situations.

Let your puppy observe at a distance, pair new experiences with things they enjoy, and keep encounters short. If they freeze, hide, try to escape, or seem overwhelmed, give them space and make the experience easier. Avoid forcing contact.

Balance infection risk with early learning

AVSAB supports safe socialisation before full vaccination, while avoiding higher-risk places such as dog parks. Ask your vet about local disease risks, safe carried outings, and contact with known healthy, vaccinated dogs.

AVSAB says well-run classes may begin at 7–8 weeks with at least one vaccine set given at least seven days before class and an initial deworming. This is not automatic clearance: your vet and class provider must agree that their requirements and your puppy’s health make attendance appropriate.

Keep building confidence

Introduce household sounds, gentle visitors, car travel, and handling a little at a time. Good classes use rewards and let puppies take breaks. Continue positive introductions as your puppy grows rather than trying to finish a checklist in a single week.

This is a Puptime puppy care summary. Ask your vet about health, diet, and vaccination decisions. Sources and further reading are available in the written guide.

training-basics.script:
You don't need a puppy who knows a long list of tricks on day one. Start with little things that help you live together. Looking round when you say their name. Coming to you in a safe space. Settling for a moment. Getting comfortable with gentle handling and a lead.

When your puppy does something you like, reward it with food, a game, or attention they enjoy. AVSAB recommends reward-based methods for training and behaviour concerns. Frightening or painful corrections can harm their welfare and your relationship.

Keep practice short and easy. If they keep getting stuck, reduce the distractions or make the task simpler. Sometimes the missing piece is a nap, a toilet trip, or a puppy who feels less worried. Hunger can get in the way too.

While they're learning, keep hazards out of reach and teach something they can do instead. Agree on the cues and expectations with everyone at home. Choose one little success at a time, and finish while your puppy is still comfortable. Some of their measured meal allowance can work nicely as training rewards.

If you're looking for a trainer, ask what happens when a puppy is afraid or gets something wrong. Look for reward-based teaching and room to pause. If fear, distress, or aggression keeps coming up, speak to your vet and get qualified behaviour support. Increasingly forceful methods aren't the way forward.

The written guide has the sources and more detail. Your vet can help tailor this advice to your puppy.
training-basics.sourceText:
What to teach first

Useful everyday skills, rewards, and choosing a trainer.

Reward the behaviours you want

AVSAB recommends reward-based methods for training and behaviour concerns. Reward a response you like with food, play, or attention your puppy enjoys. Avoid frightening or painful corrections; these can harm welfare and your relationship.

Practise in short, easy sessions. If your puppy keeps struggling, reduce distractions or make the task simpler. Hunger, tiredness, worry, and needing the toilet can get in the way of learning.

Prioritise everyday skills

Start with responding to their name, coming when called in a safe area, settling, gentle handling, and walking comfortably with a lead. Prevent access to hazards while you teach alternatives. Use the same cues and expectations across the household.

Choose one small success at a time and finish while your puppy is still comfortable. Some of their measured meal allowance can serve as training rewards.

Get help that fits your puppy

Ask a prospective trainer what they will do if your puppy is afraid or gets something wrong. Look for reward-based teaching and opportunities to pause. Persistent fear, distress, or aggression needs a vet assessment and qualified behaviour support, rather than trying increasingly forceful methods.

This is a Puptime puppy care summary. Ask your vet about health, diet, and vaccination decisions. Sources and further reading are available in the written guide.

biting-and-chewing.script:
Those tiny puppy teeth can really make themselves known. Mouthing is common while puppies explore and play, so keep suitable toys nearby. Offer one before your hands or sleeves turn into the game. Supervise chews, take away damaged toys, and put tempting household things out of reach.

If teeth touch skin, try to stay calm. Pause the interaction, and redirect once there's a little break. If you need some space, step behind a gate briefly, then come back with a suitable activity. Shouting, physical punishment, and exciting squeals can make the situation harder.

Have a look at when it happens. Is it after a lively game? Have they been awake for a while? Do they need something? Rest and quieter activities can help, alongside safe things to chew. Try to keep everyone's response consistent.

With children, an adult needs to supervise and use barriers when needed. Managing puppy biting shouldn't fall to the child.

And if biting causes an injury, seems fearful or aggressive, or simply worries you, speak to your vet and a qualified behaviour professional. You can ask for help without waiting for it to become a bigger problem.

The written guide has the sources and more detail. Your vet can help tailor this advice to your puppy.
biting-and-chewing.sourceText:
Biting, mouthing, and chewing

Normal puppy behaviour, safe alternatives, and when to get help.

Prepare for sharp little teeth

Mouthing is common as puppies explore and play. Keep age-appropriate toys nearby and offer one before hands or clothing become the game. Supervise chews and remove damaged toys. Put tempting household objects out of reach.

Pause, redirect, and check their needs

If teeth touch skin, stay calm, pause the interaction, and redirect when there is a brief break. If necessary, step behind a gate briefly to create space, then return with a suitable activity. Avoid shouting, physical punishment, and exciting squeals.

Notice when biting increases: after exciting play, when tired, or when a need has been missed. Offer rest and calmer activities as well as safe chewing. Keep the household’s response consistent.

Children and persistent problems

Adults should supervise interactions and use barriers when needed; children should not be expected to manage puppy biting themselves. If biting causes injury, appears fearful or aggressive, or worries you, contact your vet and a qualified behaviour professional.

This is a Puptime puppy care summary. Ask your vet about health, diet, and vaccination decisions. Sources and further reading are available in the written guide.

time-alone.script:
Being alone is something your puppy needs help learning. Start with feeling comfortable resting while you're nearby. Then try a very brief separation, and come back before they get worried. A few seconds may be a perfectly sensible starting point.

Only make it longer when the previous step feels easy for them. Being able to wait between toilet trips doesn't tell you whether they're emotionally comfortable on their own. There's no age formula that guarantees that.

Before you practise, check the basics: food, water, a toilet opportunity, company, and a safe resting space. If you can, watch or record what happens during a brief absence. Pacing, repeated barking, panting, or trying to escape can be signs of distress. If you see those, make the next practice easier, rather than leaving them longer to get used to it.

Real life still happens, of course. If you need to be away longer than your puppy can currently manage, arrange help from someone you trust. A crate or a food toy won't treat separation anxiety on its own.

If your puppy keeps getting distressed, speak to your vet and look for a qualified professional who uses positive methods. You and your puppy can get support with this.

The written guide has the sources and more detail. Your vet can help tailor this advice to your puppy.
time-alone.sourceText:
Learning to spend time alone

Build comfort gradually and arrange help for longer absences.

Teach a feeling of safety

Being alone is a skill to introduce gradually. First help your puppy feel comfortable resting while you are nearby. Then try very brief separations and return before they become worried. Increase time only when the previous step is easy; a few seconds may be the right starting point.

There is no age formula that guarantees emotional comfort. A puppy who can wait between toilet trips may still struggle with separation.

Watch what happens

Use a safe resting area and meet food, water, toilet, and companionship needs first. Where possible, observe or record brief absences. Pacing, repeated barking, panting, or trying to escape can signal distress. Make the next practice easier rather than leaving them longer to get used to it.

Plan around their current ability

Arrange a trusted person to help when an absence exceeds what your puppy can currently manage. Crates and food toys do not treat separation anxiety on their own. If distress persists, speak to your vet and seek a qualified professional who uses positive methods.

This is a Puptime puppy care summary. Ask your vet about health, diet, and vaccination decisions. Sources and further reading are available in the written guide.

handling-and-grooming.script:
A full grooming session is a lot to ask of a puppy who's only just met the brush. Start much smaller. A brief touch on a paw, an ear, or around the mouth, then a reward. Let them move away, and build it up gradually. If they look worried, stop and make the next step easier.

Give them a gentle introduction to brushes and other equipment before expecting the whole routine.

Teeth are worth getting into the habit of caring for too. Blue Cross recommends daily brushing as the best way to keep them healthy. Start by helping your puppy get comfortable with gentle mouth handling. Then use a suitable dog toothbrush and dog toothpaste. Human toothpaste isn't suitable. If you're unsure how to start, ask your vet to show you.

Coats need different amounts of care. Your vet or a suitable groomer can help you work out how often to brush, and what to do about nails and ears. Introduce visits positively, with time to get used to things.

If you notice pain, bleeding, an unpleasant smell, or irritation that doesn't go away, get a vet check. More forceful handling won't sort out a health problem.

The written guide has the sources and more detail. Your vet can help tailor this advice to your puppy.
handling-and-grooming.sourceText:
Handling, grooming, and teeth

Make everyday care comfortable with small, rewarding steps.

Introduce handling gently

Practise brief touches to paws, ears, and the area around the mouth, paired with a reward. Let your puppy move away and build up gradually. Introduce brushes and other equipment before expecting a full grooming session. Stop and make the step easier if they seem worried.

Build a tooth-brushing habit

Blue Cross recommends daily tooth brushing as the best way to keep teeth healthy. Begin by helping your puppy accept gentle mouth handling, then use a suitable dog toothbrush and dog toothpaste. Do not use human toothpaste. Ask your vet to demonstrate if you are unsure.

Match care to their coat and health

Grooming needs vary by coat. Ask your vet or a suitable groomer how often to brush and how to manage nails and ears. Introduce visits positively. Pain, bleeding, an unpleasant smell, or persistent irritation needs a vet check rather than more forceful handling.

This is a Puptime puppy care summary. Ask your vet about health, diet, and vaccination decisions. Sources and further reading are available in the written guide.

first-vet-visits.script:
That first vet visit is a good chance to ask all the little questions that have been building up. Arrange an early check, and bring any vaccination, worming, and health records from the breeder or rescue.

Talk about food, growth, toilet habits, and anything you've noticed that seems unusual. Ask for a parasite-prevention plan that fits your puppy's age, weight, and where you live. Don't guess a dose.

For vaccinations, get a plan for your own puppy. The products used, previous doses, and local disease risks all affect the timetable and when protection develops. A puppy vaccination schedule you've read online, including UK guidance, might not fit your puppy or your country.

Some useful questions to take along are: Which doses are still due? When can we start public walks? What safe socialisation can we do now? And what needs to be in place before puppy classes? Put follow-up dates somewhere you'll actually see them.

As your pup grows, keep checking their body condition and food portions with your vet. Ask about microchipping, up-to-date contact details, and local identification requirements too.

One last practical job: save your vet's number and the out-of-hours number now. It's much easier to have them ready before you need them.

The written guide has the sources and more detail. Your vet can help tailor this advice to your puppy.
first-vet-visits.sourceText:
First vet visits and preventive care

Vaccination records, parasites, growth checks, and questions to ask.

Bring the records you have

Arrange an early check and bring the breeder’s or rescue’s vaccination, worming, and health records. Discuss your puppy’s diet, growth, toileting, and any symptoms. Ask about a parasite-prevention plan appropriate to their age, weight, and location; do not guess a dose.

Get an individual vaccination plan

Vaccines and the timing of protection depend on the products used, previous doses, and local risks. PDSA’s UK guidance describes a course starting in puppyhood with follow-up doses; it should not be treated as a universal timetable for every country or puppy.

Ask: Which doses are still due? When are public walks safe? Which controlled socialisation opportunities are appropriate now? What are the requirements for puppy classes? Keep follow-up dates somewhere you will see them.

Keep up with growth and identification

Review body condition and food portions as your puppy grows. Discuss microchipping, contact details, and any local identification requirements. Save your regular vet’s number and their out-of-hours service before you need them.

This is a Puptime puppy care summary. Ask your vet about health, diet, and vaccination decisions. Sources and further reading are available in the written guide.

when-to-call-a-vet.script:
If you're listening because something seems wrong with your puppy, you can call your vet now. You don't need to finish this guide first.

Trouble breathing, collapse, being unable to pee, a seizure, serious bleeding, or suspected poisoning all need immediate help from a vet or emergency clinic. A swollen, painful tummy with repeated retching is also an emergency. This isn't a complete list, so call if you're worried.

With a young puppy, ask your vet promptly about vomiting, diarrhoea, refusing food, or an unusual change in behaviour. Don't rely on an adult dog's wait-and-see advice. Vomiting alongside low energy, blood, pain, or signs of dehydration needs prompt advice too.

If your puppy might have swallowed a harmful food, medicine, plant, or object, call immediately. Don't make them vomit unless a vet tells you to. Keep the packaging, or details of what they ate and when.

When you call, have meal, pee, and poop times and any notes ready if you can. Explain what's changed and how your puppy seems right now. Your Puptime log can help with that conversation. Its patterns and reminders can't diagnose illness or tell you that everything is fine.

The written guide has the sources and more detail. Your vet can help tailor this advice to your puppy.
when-to-call-a-vet.sourceText:
When to call a vet

Recognise urgent problems and use your logs to describe a change.

Get urgent help

Contact a vet or emergency clinic immediately for trouble breathing, collapse, inability to pee, a seizure, serious bleeding, or suspected poisoning. A swollen painful abdomen with repeated retching is also an emergency. These examples are not a complete list; call if you are worried.

Do not wait for a routine to explain illness

Vomiting with low energy, blood, pain, or signs of dehydration needs prompt advice. With a young puppy, contact your vet promptly about vomiting, diarrhoea, refusing food, or an unusual change in behaviour rather than applying an adult dog’s “wait and see” advice.

If they may have swallowed a harmful food, medicine, plant, or object, call immediately. Do not induce vomiting unless a vet tells you to. Keep packaging or details of what and when they ate it.

Your log can help the conversation

Have meal, pee, and poop times and your notes ready when you call. Describe what changed and how your puppy seems now. Puptime’s patterns and reminders cannot diagnose illness or rule out a problem.

This is a Puptime puppy care summary. Ask your vet about health, diet, and vaccination decisions. Sources and further reading are available in the written guide.
